newsitem.title: UK: Britain defends EMU policy in pre-election row.
newsitem.headline: Britain defends EMU policy in pre-election row.

text.p: The government on Thursday played down a warning by Japanese carmaker Toyota that Britain could lose investment it if failed to join a single European currency in the first wave.
Toyota President Hiroshi Okuda tried to quell the growing furore he caused when he linked Britain's entry into the Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) in 1999 with building new factories in Britain.
"Toyota Motor Corporation's position regarding necessary future investment in Europe is now under study and nothing has been decided," he said in a "clarifying" statement on Thursday.
"In the same manner, future investment in the U.K. is being considered as one of many possible options. This policy remains the same and has not changed at all," he added.

But his comments did little to hose down the controversy he caused in Britain on Wednesday when he told reporters at a reception in Tokyo that Toyota would shift its European investments to continental Europe if Britain did not join EMU.
His remarks threw the ruling Conservatives, who are spilt over EMU, into new turmoil months before an election which must be held by May 22.
Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine dismissed the fuss as a storm in a tea cup and defended the government's policy. "There are big issues here that need to be clarified," he told BBC radio.

"Yesterday, it was presented as though it was a major threat to this country. But overnight the Toyota president has clarified his position to reveal that those of us who realised this was a gross overstatement yesterday were actually right."

The Conservatives have prided themselves on attracting foreign investors to Britain and have insisted on a wait-and-see policy on EMU, although the government admitted last week that it was very unlikely Britain would participate in the first wave of countries in two years' time.
Heseltine said the government would do what was best for Britain when it knew the facts on which single currency decisions were taken.

"Any businessman would applaud that decision," he said. "No one today in the top level of business would tell you whether or when the single currency is going to work. They certainly would tell you that if the economic circumstances aren't propitious they wouldn't want anything to do with it."
The opposition Labour Party, which is leading the Conservatives by up to 20 points in the latest opinion polls, said it proved the government was putting jobs at risk.
Pro-European Conservative member of parliament Edwina Currie, in whose constituency the Toyota plant is located, said Okuda's message was clear.
Conservative Eurosceptics fighting against further integration with Europe viewed Okuda's remarks as foreign interference in the upcoming election.
"What we're being offered is a warning that the future ahead could be much bleaker than it has been up till now if we refuse to be part of that European future," she told BBC television.
Toyota, one of Britain's biggest foreign investors, built 117,000 cars at its plant in Derbyshire, central England.
Japanese carmaker Nissan has also said that it would prefer Britain to join EMU, but Honda Motor claims the single European currency would not be a factor in any further investment decisions.
